Really loving all these bizarre mysteries cropping up on Mars as of late. This is one of the many reasons we need to get feet on the ground there.

We need to start digging this baby up, checking out strata, begin subterranean explorations (low gravity means we should expect to see very impressive cavern systems - combine that with extensive moisture even on the surface level = ???), go check out the mouth of Olympus Mons (is it descendable?), and more.
I agree. It'll be fun to see where they go with this, but still many years away from any real solid exploration, I would think. All we can do now is little adventures like the rovers.

It might not be that far off. SpaceX continues to stick to their goal of launching a man to Mars in 2024 even though they've had many opportunities to casually extend that. The thing that's interesting about that though is that we don't need to wait anywhere near 2024 to see if they're going to stick to it. We're not going to launch a team out there to go from zero to nothing. That launch is only happening once we have, at the minimum, proven food and other life support sustainability as well as basic habitation systems autonomously built.

Since Mars only optimally aligns once every couple of years, if they're going to stick to this date they're going to have some [literally] ground breaking payloads going during 2020. I'd expect to see food and habitation setups by then so they have time to weak and relaunch the experiments in 2022 following the inevitable unforeseen issues that will arise.

In my opinion NASA's timelines are irrelevant simply because I don't think they're going anywhere, and I think they also don't think they're going anywhere. If SpaceX succeeds with their lunar flyby next year then I'd expect to see the SLS program, which has been the keystone of all of NASA's future plans, get scrapped. And that would very much be a good riddance. Direct that funding to commercial space and we'll increase our odds of actually getting somewhere that much more.
